extracted.intended_audience: USPTO staff, patent examiners, patent quality analysts, patent policymakers, and patent policy researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical criteria for evaluating patent examination quality and for identifying patent- and examination-related characteristics that correlate with subsequent litigation and IPR petitions. Includes methodological standards for empirical studies linking examination records to post-issuance dispute outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entity size (small vs large)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entity size of the patent owner is one of the characteristics with the strongest relationship to the likelihood of subsequent litigation and IPR petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small entity status and related policies (e.g., lower small entity fees) can indirectly affect litigation rates by changing incentives to seek patent protection; entity size is defined prior to examination but can influence later dispute incidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign origin of patent owner
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patent owner is foreign versus domestic is strongly related to the likelihood of subsequent litigation and IPR petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign owners are less likely to file suit in U.S. courts; this characteristic is set before examination and thus has greater explanatory power than many examination variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation / number of domestic parent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of domestic parent or continuation applications (continuation history) is strongly associated with the likelihood a patent will be litigated or petitioned for IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuation history pre-dates examination of the child application and may affect characteristics of asserted patents; reducing need for continuations could reduce litigated patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents with more independent claims are more likely to be involved in subsequent litigation and IPRs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number of independent claims may correlate with claim scope; prior literature (Lanjouw & Schankerman) also finds litigated patents generally have more claims than controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words per independent claim (claim length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer words per independent claim (shorter independent claims) are associated with higher likelihood of litigation and IPR petitions, suggesting broader claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding other factors constant, shorter independent claims are likely broader; this is used as a proxy for claim breadth in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner GS-level (seniority/experience at allowance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Schedule (GS) level of the examiner at the time the case was allowed shows some statistical relationship to litigation/IPR institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings are ambiguous: patents allowed by lower GS-level examiners are generally less likely to be involved in litigation/IPR, but institution analyses showed mixed patterns (e.g., GS-13 less likely than GS-14 or GS-12 or below). Differences may relate to Signatory Review Program and time allotted per examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of information disclosure statements (IDSs) filed
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of IDS filings in prosecution is positively associated with the likelihood of litigation and with IPR petitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may reflect applicant selection: applicants file more IDSs for inventions they perceive as more valuable, so IDS count may be correlated with patent value rather than a causal driver of litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of examiner interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: A higher number of examiner interviews during prosecution is positively associated with subsequent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Likely reflects applicant selection/effort to expedite prosecution for valuable inventions; interviews may correlate with perceived patent value rather than causing litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-action allowance (allowed on first action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications allowed on first action (without a rejection) are less likely to be involved in subsequent infringement litigation or IPR proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-action allowances likely indicate clearer claims and less ambiguity/uncertainty, which reduces disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for Continued Examination (RCEs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing RCEs during prosecution does not show a discernible impact on the likelihood of subsequent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCEs occur during examination of a single application; study found no discernable effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of the examiner’s prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the examiner located the prior art that the PTAB later used to find claims unpatentable is an indicator of search adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In hands-on OPQA review of patents where PTAB found claims unpatentable based on art not located by examiner, reviewers considered the examiner's search deficient in 61% of those cases; however, this sample is self-selected and may not generalize to average examinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of examiner’s evaluation of prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: When examiners chose to rely on a reference for a prior art rejection, they most often did so properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OPQA hands-on review found examiners generally evaluate references appropriately when they rely on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting and formulation of rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of how examiners draft rejections (clarity, proper basis) is assessed as part of prosecution quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hands-on review considered whether rejections were properly drafted; good drafting reduces disputes and misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences in claim interpretation between examiner and PTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claim construction differences between examiner and PTAB drive PTAB unpatentability findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found such differences do not appear to be a significant driver of findings of unpatentability by PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-selection and representativeness of disputed patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigated and IPR-petitioned patents are not representative of the average patent due to multiple layers of self-selection (existence of a dispute, decisions to litigate/petition, settlement filters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any analysis of litigated/IPR patents must account for self-selection; results should be interpreted cautiously and not generalized to all patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of matched case-control design (matching variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Matched case-control studies should match litigated/IPR patents to controls on variables (e.g., month of application filing and IPC subclass) to reduce confounding and increase statistical efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching on application month and IPC subclass follows prior literature (Lanjouw & Schankerman) and helps construct appropriate control groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conditional logistic regression for matched samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditional logistic regression is the statistical method used to estimate relationships between explanatory variables and the binary outcome (litigated or not; petitioned for IPR or not) in matched case-control studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistic regression is appropriate for categorical binary outcomes; conditional variant accounts for matched strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of PALM and internal USPTO prosecution data
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution variables should be drawn from the PALM system (dates, office actions, IDS filings, RCEs, examiner assignments, GAU/TC, docket placement) for accurate measurement of examination characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PALM contains detailed communications and internal processing information that are essential for linking prosecution features to later dispute outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hands-on OPQA review using a structured questionnaire
rubrics_metrics.description: A hands-on review of prosecution history by OPQA specialists using a standardized questionnaire to assess elements such as prior art search adequacy, evaluation of references, and quality of rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix II provides the questionnaire used by QA specialists; structured review complements statistical analysis by qualitatively evaluating examination actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward and backward citations, and citation-based measures of patent value
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward citations and citations per claim are indicators of patent value and are associated with higher litigation rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward citations are commonly used as proxy for patent value; litigated patents tend to have more forward citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-issuance indicators of patent value (maintenance fees, reexamination, ownership change, collateralization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquired/post-issuance characteristics — change in ownership, reexamination, payment of maintenance fees, collateralization — predict higher likelihood of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are later signals of continued investment/value in a patent and correlate with being litigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology area / classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation and IPR rates vary substantially across technology areas (e.g., software, telecommunications, financial patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different tech centers and IPC subclasses have different baseline litigation propensities; analyses should control for technology area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent portfolio effects (assignee patent holdings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A larger patent portfolio reduces the probability of suing on any individual patent in the portfolio, especially for smaller firms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portfolio holdings and concentration in technology areas affect incentives to litigate and to settle; consider assignee-level patenting context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner hours per disposal / time spent examining
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased examiner hours per disposal (time spent examining) is correlated with decreased later litigation rates for patents issued by that examination group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior work (King 2003) found that more examination time per application is associated with lower litigation; implies examination effort may improve downstream quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of references cited on IDS and potential search overload
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation of a large number of references on IDS may impede the examiner’s ability to identify the most relevant prior art, affecting search adequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High IDS reference counts may make it harder for examiners to find the most relevant references; this may contribute to references being omitted from the examiner’s search that PTAB later uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of changes in substantive law when evaluating prosecution quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in substantive patent law (e.g., obviousness standards) over time affect how examination records should be interpreted relative to later litigation or IPR outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents issued under earlier law may be litigated under changed standards; evaluations of examination quality must account for contemporaneous law and USPTO guidance in effect at issuance.
